rationale: The note treats note atomicity as an unqualified good, but a defensible tradition holds that aggressive atomization fragments arguments whose force depends on their connective tissue. The counter-position has real adherents and vault evidence; the risk is that it overstates how often connective notes actually get read.

counter_note.proposed_title: Against: Every note should contain exactly one idea
counter_note.central_counter_claim: Strict one-idea atomicity can destroy the argumentative structure that makes a set of ideas more than the sum of its parts.
counter_note.body: The atomicity rule is sold as pure upside: small notes link better, recombine better, decay slower. But an argument is not a bag of claims — it is claims held in a particular relation. Split the relation across three atomic notes and the link graph records that they are related while losing *how*. The reader who follows the links reconstructs a sequence the author never has to defend as a whole. Atomicity optimizes for retrieval and recombination at the cost of the one thing a sustained argument needs: a place where its steps are committed to in order, where a weak inference cannot hide behind a wikilink.

engages_with.original_quote: Every note should contain exactly one idea.
engages_with.counter: An argument's load-bearing content is often the relation between ideas, not the ideas themselves; 'exactly one idea' has no place to put that relation, so it silently drops it.

counter_evidence.supports: An earlier note where the author credits a breakthrough to writing a single long, sequential argument rather than atomic fragments.
A note observing that the author's most-linked atomic notes are rarely revisited as a connected chain.

concedes: For reference material and reusable definitions, atomicity genuinely does improve linking and reuse, exactly as the note claims.
Atomic notes decay more gracefully because each can be updated in isolation.
counter_note.real_world_adherents: Writers in the rhetoric and composition tradition who treat argument structure as primary; critics of pure Zettelkasten practice who argue it favors collection over composition.
